name: St. Stephen's Cathedral
label: St. Stephen's Cathedra
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Stephansplatz' (3 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Stephansplatz' (node/4560869722): point.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/212496461: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Saint Stephen's Cathedral' (143 m across).
notes: Gothic cathedral with a patterned tile roof in the heart of the old city.

text.description:
St. Stephen's Cathedral, known locally as the Stephansdom, is the mother church of the Archdiocese of Vienna and the city's most important religious building. The first church on the site was dedicated in 1147. The Gothic building you see today grew mainly from the work started under Duke Rudolf IV in the 14th century. Its multi-coloured tiled roof is one of the best-known sights in Vienna, and the south tower, nicknamed the "Steffl", reaches 136 metres. The cathedral is about 107 metres long. Much of the stonework is dark from centuries of soot, though some areas have been cleaned back to a paler colour. The roof was badly damaged by fire in April 1945 and the cathedral fully reopened in 1952.

It photographs well because the Gothic west façade rises straight out of an open square. That gives you room to step back and fit the whole front, with the patterned roof above it. From the front you can capture the tall tower, the carved doorway and the zigzag roof tiles in one frame. The square is very busy for most of the day, so go early if you want a cleaner shot. If the main view is crowded, try the corner at Stock-im-Eisen-Platz for an angled view with the spire, or Jasomirgottstraße for the entrance framed by a narrow street. The South Tower climb is a paid activity, so check the official site for tower access details before you go.
text.geographic_location: St. Stephen's Cathedral stands on Stephansplatz in the heart of Vienna's old city centre (the Innere Stadt, or 1st district). The square wraps around the cathedral's west front.
text.directions_text: Head for Stephansplatz in the middle of Vienna's old city. From there it is about 1 minute on foot to the middle of the building. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to fit the full west façade and roof from close range. Then switch to the default lens (1x) for a more natural look, and use telephoto/zoom (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for the roof tiles and tower details.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Stephansplatz (in front of the main west entrance). The cathedral's Gothic west façade and tiled roof, framed by the open square. From here you see the Gothic west façade and tiled roof framed by the open square, with the cathedral to the east of you.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and hold the phone upright and level, so the towers don't lean. Leave a little open sky above the roof and some square in front to give a sense of scale. For a different view, try the corner at Stock-im-Eisen-Platz, which shows the spire and façade together, or Jasomirgottstraße, where the narrow street frames the entrance and cuts out much of the crowd.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the brightest part of the façade to focus, then lower the exposure slider slightly so the sky and roof tiles keep their colour. Take the 0.5x shot first, then zoom in for close-ups of the roof.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning, when the square is quieter and the first light hits the roof tiles. Midday is the busiest time.

text.access_note: The square is open public space, but entry to the cathedral and tower access may be restricted or ticketed (the South Tower climb is paid), so check the official site before you go.

name: Schönbrunn Palace
label: Schönbrunn Palace
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Gloriette' (4 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Gloriette' (way/22893165): middle (135 m across); moved 10 m off buildings.

notes: Baroque imperial summer residence with formal gardens.

text.description: Schönbrunn is the Habsburgs' old summer palace, a yellow Baroque building with 1,441 rooms, set in the 13th district of Vienna. It became a World Heritage Site in 1996, together with its gardens. The classic photograph is not taken at the palace door. It is taken from the Gloriette, the colonnaded building on the hill at the end of the garden axis, which has stood there since 1775. From its upper terrace the yellow palace and the formal gardens lie in front of you, with the Vienna skyline behind them. That layered view is what makes the shot work on a phone: lawns and clipped hedges in the foreground, the palace in the middle, the city beyond. The hill is about 60 metres high, which is enough to look down the whole length of the gardens. Guides say the view is best late in the day, while others suggest arriving early to avoid the crowds, so choose whichever suits your day. If you also want a straight-on picture of the building, the Ehrenhof, the courtyard in front of the palace, shows the symmetrical front facade and its central gateway filling the frame. Photography is not allowed inside the state rooms, so both of these pictures are taken outdoors.
text.geographic_location: Schönbrunn Palace is in Hietzing, Vienna's 13th district. The Gloriette stands on the hill at the far end of the palace gardens, to the south of the palace.
text.directions_text: No nearby station or tram stop is listed for this spot, so check local transport options yourself for getting to Schönbrunn Palace in Hietzing. From the palace, walk south up through the gardens towards the Gloriette on the hill. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x), which gives a natural view of the whole garden and palace. If you want to pick the palace out from the skyline behind it, try 2x or 3x on a phone with a telephoto lens. Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) only if you want the terrace's columns or arches in the frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand at Gloriette (upper terrace, looking back south-northwest down the garden axis toward the palace). The yellow palace and formal gardens in the foreground, with the Vienna skyline behind them. From here, turn round and look back north down the garden axis. The palace is straight ahead of you, with the yellow building and formal gardens in the foreground and the Vienna skyline behind.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and put the palace on the central vertical line so the garden paths lead the eye towards it. Keep a little of the terrace edge or a column in one corner if you want a sense of height. For a second picture, the Ehrenhof in front of the palace gives a symmetrical, face-on view of the front facade, so keep the phone level and the gateway in the centre.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the palace to focus, then slide the exposure down slightly so the sky keeps its colour and the yellow walls do not wash out. A panorama can capture the full width of the gardens, but move slowly.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: One hour before sunset, or early morning before the crowds arrive.

text.access_note: The Gloriette terrace is reached on foot and guides describe it as free to reach, but opening hours can vary, so check the official site before you go; the Ehrenhof may also be closed for works or events, so check that too.

name: Hofburg
label: Hofburg
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Michaelerplatz' (4 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Michaelerplatz' (relation/2979377): middle (68 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap relation/3898175: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Hofburg Palace' (598 m across).
notes: Former imperial palace with the grand dome facing Heldenplatz.

text.description:
The Hofburg was the main palace of the Habsburg dynasty and is still in daily use: since 1946 it has been the official residence and workplace of Austria's president. It is less a single building than a sprawl of wings added over centuries, starting with the oldest parts in the 13th century and finishing with the Neue Burg, built between 1881 and 1913. That mix of styles is why it rewards a slow walk with your phone out.

From the middle of this semicircular square you can look through the central archway at the Michaelertrakt façade and its dome, with the glass-covered Roman excavation in the foreground. Guides often call it the iconic Hofburg shot, and the dome is the most-photographed view of the palace.

If you want something wider and more open, Heldenplatz shows the long Neue Burg façade with an equestrian statue in front. The Burggarten gives a softer view, with the Mozart statue and its treble-clef flower bed in front of the Neue Burg roofline.

The square fills with people and carriages later in the day, so go early if you want a clear frame. Take a few steps sideways to line the dome up in the middle of the arch, and keep the phone level so the verticals stay straight.
text.geographic_location: The Hofburg sits in the centre of Vienna, facing Heldenplatz. Michaelerplatz is the semicircular square at its edge.
text.directions_text: The map lists no public transport stop for this spot, so walk from the centre of Vienna's old town to Michaelerplatz. Once you are the middle of the palace complex lies to the south, about 3 minutes on foot. To reach Heldenplatz and the Neue Burg, keep walking through the palace grounds. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Michaelerplatz (centre of the semicircular square, or the outer edge facing the Michaelertor). The Michaelertrakt façade and its dome framed through the central archway, with the Roman excavation glass in the foreground. In the centre of the semicircular square or at the outer edge facing the Michaelertor. From there you see the Michaelertrakt façade and its dome framed through the central archway, with the Roman excavation glass in the foreground. The middle of the wider palace complex lies to the south of you.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Switch on gridlines and put the archway in the centre so the dome sits symmetrically inside it. Keep the glass of the excavation along the bottom of the frame to add depth. For a more open view, walk on to Heldenplatz for the Neue Burg with its equestrian statue, or to the Burggarten for the Mozart statue and flower bed in front of the roofline.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the dome to focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the sky does not wash out the detail. Hold the phone level to keep the vertical lines straight, and use the 0.5x lens only when you need the width, as it can stretch the edges of the frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Before 8am, when the square is emptiest. Later it fills with people and carriages.

text.access_note: Michaelerplatz and the other outside viewpoints are public squares and gardens, but the interiors, museums and treasury are separate attractions where photography may be restricted, so check the official site before you go.

name: Belvedere
label: Belvedere
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Unteres Belvedere' (2 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Unteres Belvedere' (way/31313338): middle (146 m across); moved 10 m off buildings.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/546340540: large area 'Belvedere' (1149 m across): previous pin kept, it lies inside.
notes: Baroque palace with a reflecting pond and a view over the city.

text.description:
The Belvedere is a pair of Baroque palaces, the Upper and the Lower, linked by a formal garden. Prince Eugene of Savoy built it as a summer residence, and the Upper Belvedere was completed in 1723. The garden was laid out in the French style by Dominique Girard, with symmetrical lawns, water basins, steps, cascades, clipped hedges and statues, spread over three terraces. The Upper Belvedere is also the building on the Austrian 20-cent euro coin.

The palace photographs well because the garden gives you a long, orderly view with plenty to place in front of it. The classic shot is the palace mirrored in the pool, taken from the Upper Belvedere side. A quieter alternative is to start at the far end of the park, at the Unteres Belvedere, and shoot back up the garden. From there the statues and trees give you foreground, and a longer lens pulls the palace in so it feels closer and more compact.

Keep the palace centred and the gardens symmetrical, and turn on your gridlines so the roofline stays level. Walk a few steps sideways to line a statue up against the facade. The garden and the pool are free to enter, but the palace interiors are ticketed, so check the official site before you go if you plan to go inside. The fountains usually run only in the frost-free months, roughly April to October, so in winter the water features may be switched off.
text.geographic_location: The Belvedere is in Vienna's third district, Landstraße, on the south-eastern edge of the historic centre. The garden runs between the Lower and Upper palaces, just south of the Rennweg.
text.directions_text: Head for the Landstraße district and ask for the Unteres Belvedere, the Lower Belvedere end of the park. Walk through the garden in that direction, which takes about 5 minutes on foot. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Use telephoto (2x to 5x, depending on your phone) for the compressed view of the palace from the far end of the park. The default lens (1x) also works if you want the whole garden in the frame. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) only if you move closer to the pool.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand at Unteres Belvedere (north end of the park, shooting back toward the Upper Belvedere with a longer lens). The main Upper Belvedere building framed across the garden from the far end, with statues and trees as foreground. Face south and shoot back toward the Upper Belvedere. The main palace building sits across the garden, with statues and trees as foreground.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and put the palace on the central vertical line, with the roofline level. Use a statue or a tree branch at the edge of the frame as foreground. Zoom in until the palace fills about a third of the frame width. For a second, classic view, walk up to the Oberes Belvedere and shoot the palace's Baroque facade mirrored in the pool, using the default lens (1x) or ultra-wide (0.5x).
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the palace to focus, then slide the exposure down slightly so the sky does not wash out the facade. If the pool is still, keep your phone steady and shoot a few frames, as ripples ruin the reflection.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning is best, because there are fewer people than later in the day, and crowds tend to build after about 10 am. Golden hour or late evening can also work if you prefer warmer light.

text.access_note: The garden and the pool are free to enter, but the palace interiors are ticketed, so check the official site before you go for opening times and tickets.

name: Vienna State Opera
label: State Opera
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Albertinaplatz' (4 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Albertinaplatz' (way/55970609): middle (75 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/8097595: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Vienna State Opera' (171 m across).
notes: Neo-Renaissance opera house on the Ringstraße.

text.description:
The Vienna State Opera is a big, pale Renaissance Revival building on the Ringstrasse, the ring road around Vienna's old centre. It was the first major building on the Ring, built between 1861 and 1869, and it opened with Mozart's Don Giovanni in May 1869. It seats 1,709 people. Most of the interior was destroyed by fire in March 1945, but the front section survived, including the main stairways and the foyer. The auditorium was rebuilt afterwards in a style close to the original. That history is why the facade still looks so complete today.

It photographs well because the front is wide, symmetrical and richly detailed, with arches and stonework that catch the light. A classic view, named by most guides, is from Albertinaplatz, on the raised Albertina terrace by the museum entrance. From there you look down across the street at the full facade, with the Ringstrasse scene below and the Archduke Albrecht statue close by. The height also helps you avoid the tram wires that clutter shots taken from the front. If you want a straight-on view with the Pegasus statues and tram light trails at night, try Opernring. Operngasse may give a quieter side view, but check it on site.

Keep your phone level and use the gridlines so the tall walls stay upright. Leave a little space around the building, because you can always crop later.

Switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) only if you have to stand close, and keep the building centred to limit leaning walls. Use telephoto (2x-3x) for details such as the arches and the stonework.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Albertinaplatz (raised Albertina terrace by the museum entrance, across the street from the opera). shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the facade to focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly so the sky stays deep blue and the stone keeps its detail. At blue hour, hold the phone steady against a wall or railing and let night mode do its work.

camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Karlsplatz' (4 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Karlsplatz' (node/3503264091): point.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/8097149: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Karlskirche' (99 m across).
notes: Baroque church with a huge green dome and twin columns.

text.description:
The Karlskirche (Charles Church) is a Baroque church on Karlsplatz, with a green dome and a columned porch that look wonderful on a phone screen. Emperor Charles VI promised to build it in 1713, a year after the last big plague epidemic in Vienna, and dedicated it to Saint Charles Borromeo, who was revered as a healer of plague sufferers. Building began in 1716 and finished in 1737. The front mixes a temple-style portico with two tall freestanding columns covered in spiral reliefs, inspired by Trajan's Column in Rome. Those columns and the dome give you strong shapes to work with.

The classic picture is taken from the pool side of Karlsplatz, looking at the church front. The shallow reflecting pool mirrors the façade and dome, and the twin columns frame the scene. It only works when the pool has water in it, which is in the warmer months, and when the surface is still, so sunrise, dusk or blue hour are the best moments. Standing on the far side of the pool puts the reflection in the foreground. Check the columns before you plan the shot: one was recently reported to be under scaffolding, which could spoil the symmetry.

If the pool is empty or crowded, try Resselpark for a wider view across the small pond. The Wien Museum also gives a higher view of the whole church with the square below, reached through the museum.
text.geographic_location: The Karlskirche stands on Karlsplatz in central Vienna, on the border between the Wieden district and the Innere Stadt (the city centre).

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the church front to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly so the sky and the green dome keep their colour. At blue hour, use night mode and brace your elbows against your body to keep the shot steady.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Sunrise or dusk, when the water is still. Blue hour is a good choice for the lit-up church. The reflection is only possible in warmer seasons, when the pool is filled.

text.description: The Albertina is a museum in Vienna's Innere Stadt, right beside the Hofburg. It is best known for its print room, which holds roughly 65,000 drawings and about a million old master prints. It also shows Impressionist and modern art and runs temporary exhibitions. The building stands on a surviving stretch of the old city defences, the Augustinian Bastion. It was once a palace for the Habsburg Duke Albert of Teschen, took the name Albertina in 1921, and was heavily damaged in March 1945 before being rebuilt. A distinctive modern roof by Hans Hollein over the entrance area was finished in 2008. From there you look across to the State Opera, with Burggarten and the Hofburg to one side. The height gives you a cleaner angle on the Opera than you would get from street level. You do not need a museum ticket to stand on the terrace. If you want the Albertina's own facade, walk to Albrechtsbrunnen, the wall fountain across the street, for a close, ground-level view. Burggarten is a pleasant alternative, but it shows mostly the Hofburg and the lawns, with the Albertina only a small part of the frame.

text.description: The Kunsthistorisches Museum is Vienna's great art museum, and its building is as much of a subject as the paintings inside. It is a palatial, sandstone Renaissance Revival block on the Ring Road, with large arched windows and an octagonal dome about 60 metres high. It was built between 1871 and 1891 to plans by Gottfried Semper and Karl von Hasenauer. Emperor Franz Joseph I commissioned it, together with its near-twin the Natural History Museum across Maria-Theresien-Platz, to house the Habsburgs' art collection and open it to the public. The two buildings mirror each other, which is why the area suits balanced, symmetrical photos. The building has plenty of detail to work with: the long run of arched windows, the carved stonework and the dome rising above the roofline. If you go inside, the grand stairway is decorated with paintings by Gustav Klimt, Ernst Klimt, Franz Matsch, Hans Makart and Mihály Munkácsy. Check the official site for visiting details before you go. Outside, the building is very large, so decide early whether you want the whole façade or a detail. Take a wide shot first, then move in for a closer picture of the windows, the stonework or the dome. Keep your phone level so the tall walls don't lean inwards, and look for a clear gap in the crowd before you shoot.
text.geographic_location: In central Vienna, on the Ring Road (Ringstraße), facing Maria-Theresien-Platz. The Natural History Museum stands directly opposite.

name: Naschmarkt
label: Naschmarkt
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Linke Wienzeile' (2 web pages); placed at the stretch of Linke Wienzeile nearest the subject (our map tiles).

notes: Long open-air market with food stalls and cafés.

text.description:
The Naschmarkt is a popular fruit and vegetable market in Vienna, with rows of stalls selling fresh produce, herbs, cheese, bread, meat and fish, plus small restaurants tucked in between. It stretches for roughly a kilometre and a half along the Wien River. It began as the Aschenmarkt, a name that stuck until around 1820, when people started calling it the Naschmarkt. The first pavilions over the river went up in 1902. On Saturdays a flea market spreads along the neighbouring stretch, as it has since 1977.

It photographs well because everything is close and colourful: piled produce, hand-written signs, spice sacks and busy aisles. Behind the stalls, the Otto Wagner apartment buildings with their Jugendstil (Viennese Art Nouveau) details give you a handsome backdrop. The classic street-level shot is from the middle of the market near the antique stalls, looking along the aisle with those houses rising behind.

For best results, take a few wide pictures of the whole scene and then step closer for the details, such as a pyramid of olives, a spice display or a pastry counter. Stallholders are busy people, so ask before you photograph them up close, and keep to the edge of the aisle so you don't block shoppers.
text.geographic_location: The Naschmarkt runs along the Wienzeile in central Vienna, over the Wien River, with the Otto Wagner apartment buildings facing it. Its eastern end meets Karlsplatz, where Wagner's Stadtbahn pavilions stand.
text.directions_text: There is no station or tram stop right at this spot, so navigate on the map to Linke Wienzeile or the Karlsplatz area at the market's eastern end, then follow the stalls west along the Wienzeile. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

Stalls spilling along the market aisle with the Otto Wagner apartment buildings rising behind them. shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and put the aisle on one of the lower lines, with the Wagner houses filling the top third. Hold the phone level so the building edges stay straight. Stalls or hanging goods at the edge of the frame add depth. For a different angle, a higher view down the stall rows may be possible from a terrace above the market, and the Karlsplatz pavilions frame the eastern entrance; both are worth a look if you have time.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the brightest part of the scene to focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the colours stay rich and the sky doesn't wash out. Use portrait mode for close shots of food, and ask permission before photographing vendors.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Saturday morning gives the busiest, liveliest atmosphere, with the flea market in full swing. Weekday mornings are quieter if you want clearer aisles.

text.description: The Graben is one of Vienna's best-known streets, a broad pedestrian promenade in the first district lined with grand shopfronts and façades. It photographs well because it is long and fairly straight, so you get a strong sense of depth with rows of buildings leading the eye along it. The name means 'ditch'. It goes back to the Roman camp of Vindobona, where a trench ran in front of the settlement wall. At the end of the 12th century the Babenberg dukes filled the trench in, paid for with the ransom collected for Richard the Lionheart. In the 18th century the Graben became the fashionable place to promenade, and in 1974 it became Vienna's first pedestrian zone, at first on a provisional basis. For the classic view, stand at the Stephansplatz end and look back down the street. The long perspective is the main picture here, and the Baroque Plague Column makes a good foreground subject if you walk about 250 m (around 4 minutes) along the street. A second option is the corner where the Graben meets Kohlmarkt, which lets you frame the Hofburg dome at the end of Kohlmarkt with shopfronts at the edge of the picture. Go early if you can, because the street is much emptier in the morning. Keep your phone straight and level so the tall façades do not lean, and watch for delivery vehicles in the early hours.

The Graben itself is about 4 minutes' walk away if you want the Plague Column in the foreground. For the Hofburg dome, try the corner of Graben and Kohlmarkt as an alternative.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and put the centre of the street on the middle line so the façades balance on both sides. Crouch slightly or hold the phone at chest height to keep the vertical lines straight. If you walk along the street, use the Plague Column as a foreground subject with the street stretching away behind it. From the Kohlmarkt corner, place the Hofburg dome at the end of the street and let the Graben's shopfronts fill the edge of the frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the street in the middle distance to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly if the sky is bright, so the façade details do not wash out. If people are crossing, a Live Photo lets you pick the cleanest frame afterwards.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning, when there are fewer people and the street looks cleaner. Delivery vehicles may still be about at that time.

notes: Colourful apartment block with an uneven, irregular façade.

text.description:
The Hundertwasserhaus is an apartment house in the Landstraße district, completed in 1985 after the ideas of the Austrian artist Friedensreich Hundertwasser. It looks nothing like the streets around it. The floors undulate, the roof is covered in earth and grass, and trees grow out of the rooms, with branches reaching out of the windows. Inside there are 53 apartments and a total of 250 trees and bushes, so the facade is a patchwork of colours, wavy lines and greenery.

It suits a phone well because the whole building is one bold, busy picture. This is the classic frame: far enough back to fit the full building in, with the rooftop trees above and the rolling pavement in front of you. If you want a different angle, the Hundertwasser Village terrace gives a raised view across the street. Check the exact access point when you arrive.

The house is a private home, so you cannot go in. Please keep the pavement clear, because the street is narrow, and don't photograph into windows or onto balconies. Once you have your wide shot, walk along Kegelgasse for close-ups of the tiles, mirrors and window frames, and for the view where the house meets the ordinary nineteenth-century buildings either side.
text.geographic_location: In Vienna's Landstraße district, on the corner of Kegelgasse and Löwengasse.
text.directions_text: No Underground or tram stop is listed for this spot, so use the map to navigate to the corner of Kegelgasse and Löwengasse in the Landstraße district. The house is then about 1 minute on foot away to the east. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

Then switch to the default lens (1x) for the building without stretched edges. Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for details such as tiles, mirrors and window frames.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand at the corner of Kegelgasse and Löwengasse (south corner, across the street from the facade). The whole patchwork facade, with rooftop trees and the rolling pavement in the foreground, framed from the corner. Stand on Kegelgasse, on the south corner across the street from the facade. The house is to the east of you. Stay on the pavement and keep it clear for others.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and keep the vertical lines of the neighbouring buildings straight so the picture doesn't lean. Leave a strip of the wavy pavement at the bottom and the rooftop trees at the top. For a raised alternative, try the Hundertwasser Village terrace if you can reach it, or walk along Kegelgasse for close-up details.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on a brightly coloured wall to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly if the sky is washing out the top of the picture. Hold the phone level and still before you press the shutter.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning, before the tour groups arrive around mid-morning. The street is quieter then and easier to photograph.

text.description: The Musikverein is Vienna's famous concert hall, home to the Vienna Philharmonic since it opened on 6 January 1870. Emperor Franz Joseph I granted the land during the building of the Ringstraße, and the Danish-born architect Theophil Hansen designed it in the style of an ancient Greek temple. That calm, symmetrical, classical look suits a phone camera well: strong straight lines, tall columns and a clear, balanced front. Inside is the Golden Hall (Goldener Saal), known for its acoustics and for the annual Vienna New Year's Concert, but this spot is about the outside. The main entrance faces Musikvereinsplatz, between Karlsplatz and Bösendorferstraße, and the building sits behind the Hotel Imperial, which fronts the Kärntner Ring. Step back where the pavement allows, or switch to the ultra-wide lens. Keep the phone level, using the gridlines, so the columns and rooflines stay straight. Then move in for details such as the columns, the figures and the entrance. Pedestrians and traffic will often be in the foreground, so wait a moment for a clearer frame.

notes: Twin-spired neo-Gothic church near the university.

text.description:
The Votive Church is a neo-Gothic church on Vienna's Ringstraße, built in white sandstone with two slim spires, three gabled doorways and a big rose window. It was funded by donations as a thank-you after Emperor Franz Joseph survived an assassination attempt in 1853. Building began in 1856 and the church was dedicated on 24 April 1879, the couple's silver jubilee. The architect, Heinrich von Ferstel, was only 26 when he won the competition. It looks medieval, but it is far younger than Stephansdom, which visitors often confuse it with.

It photographs well because the whole front is symmetrical, with the twin spires giving strong vertical lines against the sky. It is also set back from the road, behind open green space, so you can step away from it. The best result comes from the park beside the church, facing the facade, where you get both spires in one frame with room around them. A first-time visitor will find it easy to line up. Sigmund-Freud-Park is a good second try: trees frame the spires, and in spring magnolia blossom can sit in the foreground. Bloom times vary, so check before you go. The front is sometimes covered by advertising banners, so have a look at the facade first. For a different angle, Frankgasse gives a symmetrical street view with the towers at the end.
text.geographic_location: The church stands on the Ringstraße in central Vienna, set back behind Sigmund-Freud-Park.
text.directions_text: No Underground or tram stops are listed for this spot, so go by taxi or hired scooter to the Ringstraße in the city centre, where the church stands just back from the boulevard. Votivpark, beside the church, is the recommended place to step back and frame the facade. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

If you walk further back, switch to the default lens (1x) for a more natural look with less stretching at the edges. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for details such as the rose window and the statue gallery above the doorways.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Votivpark (park beside the church, facing the facade). The full neo-Gothic front of the church with both spires, framed by open space and a clean view of the facade. shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and line up the central doorway with the middle vertical line, so the two spires sit evenly on each side. Hold the phone upright and level, and keep the whole facade in frame, with a little sky above the spires. For a second view, try Sigmund-Freud-Park, with trees or blossom framing the spires, or Frankgasse, where the street leads the eye to the towers.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the facade to set focus, then slide the exposure down a touch so the white stone keeps its detail and the sky is not washed out. Use telephoto for close details rather than cropping later.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Soft light early or late in the day is kinder to pale stone than harsh midday sun. An evenly cloudy sky also works well. If you want spring blossom in Sigmund-Freud-Park, check the bloom on the day, as the timing varies.

text.description: Vienna City Hall is the town hall of the city, a Gothic Revival building designed by Friedrich von Schmidt and built between 1872 and 1883. It stands off the Ringstrasse, and its front is built for photographs. A tall central tower, 98 metres high and topped by the Rathausmann figure, is flanked by four smaller towers. Open arcades run along the ground floor. The whole building is about 152 metres long and 127 metres wide, so it is far too big to take in from close up. Stepping back onto the square gives you the full width and the symmetry of the front. The stonework is also unusually crisp, because the façade was restored between 2012 and 2023. Look for the three equestrian statues above the central entrances and the row of citizen-soldier statues along the front balustrade. They make good details if you want a closer shot after the wide one. Start in the middle of Rathausplatz and look west, with the tower centred. Then move to the edge of Rathauspark, where trees and fountains can frame the foreground. The square often hosts events such as a winter Christmas market and a summer film festival, and these can block or crowd the classic view. If so, try the park side instead.
text.geographic_location: Vienna City Hall is in the Innere Stadt on Rathausplatz, just off the Ringstrasse. Rathauspark lies in front of it, and Florianipark is behind.
text.directions_text: No stations or tram stops are listed for this spot, so head for the Innere Stadt and the Ringstrasse, then look for Rathausplatz. Walk towards the tower and you will reach the arcades at the front. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for the clock tower, the Rathausmann and the statues above the entrance.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Rathausplatz (middle of the square, facing the main façade). The full front of the City Hall with its central clock tower and flanking spires. For an alternative, Rathauspark shows the clock tower and the four smaller towers framed by trees and fountains. The Volksgarten shows the City Hall through trees and flower beds, often with the Theseus Temple in the same frame.

shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning gives softer light and fewer people in the square. Some people prefer the evening, when the building is lit, so you could try both.

notes: Greek Revival building with the Athena fountain in front.

text.description:
The Austrian Parliament Building is where Austria's two houses of parliament meet, and it is one of the largest buildings on the Ringstraße, covering over 13,500 square metres. The architect Theophil Hansen designed it in a Greek Revival style, chosen because ancient Greece was linked with the ideal of democracy. The foundation stone was laid in 1874 and the building was finished in 1883. After five years of renovation it reopened in 2023.

It photographs well because the tall columns and the long roofline give you strong, clean lines, and the Pallas Athena fountain stands right in front as a ready-made foreground. The fountain was made by Carl Kundmann from Hansen's plans, between 1898 and 1902. Viennese humour says Athena turned her back on the building in disgust at the squabbling inside, which is a nice story to tell with your photo.

For an easy first picture, stand by the fountain and let the statue and the fountain figures sit at the bottom of the frame, with the columns and roofline behind them. If you want a different angle, the Volksgarten gives a view through the rose beds with the Theseus Temple. The Dr.-Karl-Renner-Ring gives a slightly angled view with the City Hall tower behind, which suits zoom. Restoration work nearby means scaffolding or fencing may hide parts of the façade, so be ready to adjust your angle.
text.geographic_location: The Parliament Building stands on the Ringstraße in Vienna's first district, Innere Stadt, near Hofburg Palace and the Palace of Justice. The Volksgarten and the Rathaus (City Hall) are close by.

The building's Corinthian façade and roofline framed by the Athena statue and the fountain figures in the foreground. Keep the phone level so the vertical lines stay straight. For a different view, try the Volksgarten, where the façade is framed by the rose beds and the Theseus Temple.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the sky or the façade to set focus and exposure, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the bright stone keeps its detail. Take a few frames in case people walk into the shot.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Check how the light falls on the façade when you arrive and adjust your timing to suit. Evening light also suits the angled view from the Dr.-Karl-Renner-Ring.

text.description:
The Mozarthaus Vienna, also called the Figaro House, is the only surviving Viennese home of Mozart, who lived here from 1784 to 1787. It stands at Domgasse 5 in the Old Town, close to St. Stephen's Cathedral, and is now a museum. The building dates from the 17th century and was redeveloped in 1716. Mozart composed The Marriage of Figaro while living on the first floor.

For a phone photo, the best subject is the outside of the building seen from the narrow lane. The facade sits among the older Old Town buildings of Domgasse, so the picture says 'Vienna' without needing much else in the frame. Today the house is entered from the rear on Domgasse, so the lane is also where you will see visitors arriving. If you go inside, photography may be restricted, so look at the signs and ask staff.

Stand in the lane and keep the phone level, with the gridlines switched on, so the vertical lines of the facade stay straight. The lane is tight, so the whole front may not fit at the default lens (1x). Try the ultra-wide (0.5x) and step back as far as you comfortably can. Then try a second shot with the telephoto (2x or more) to pick out a doorway or window detail. Morning or late afternoon light suits the exterior best.

name: Burgtheater

camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Rathausplatz' (3 web pages); placed at our map tiles: 'Rathausplatz / Burgtheater' (pois).

text.description:
The Burgtheater is the national theatre of Austria and one of the most important German-language stages. Vienna people simply call it "die Burg". The company began in 1741 under Empress Maria Theresa, in a building beside the Hofburg palace. The theatre you see today moved to the Ringstraße and opened on 14 October 1888, designed by Gottfried Semper and Karl Freiherr von Hasenauer. It was largely destroyed in March 1945 and rebuilt between 1953 and 1955. Inside, frescoes by Gustav Klimt, Ernst Klimt and Franz von Matsch show the history of theatre.

For a photo, the big draw is the front of the building, with its curved wings and columns. From Rathausplatz, across the Ring, the lower façade is framed by the open town hall square and fills the view over the Ringstraße. That makes it a straightforward phone shot: you can stand still, keep the whole front in one frame and let the open space around you do the work. After dark the façade is lit, which is a favourite time for photos here.

Two things to bear in mind. In colder months a winter ice rink on the square may block part of the view. And photography is not allowed inside during performances, so the outdoor views are the practical choice. If the square is busy, try Universitätsring for the full front with a tram passing in the foreground, or the edge of the Volksgarten for the theatre seen through greenery.
text.geographic_location: The Burgtheater stands on the Ringstraße in central Vienna, beside the Volksgarten and not far from the Hofburg. The town hall square is directly opposite, across the Ring.
text.directions_text: Head for the Ringstraße in central Vienna and ask for Rathausplatz, the square opposite the Burgtheater. Stand on the Rathausplatz side of the Ring. The theatre is to the north-east, about 2 minutes on foot if you want to walk over to it afterwards. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the whole façade. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) if the square is crowded or you want to include more of the open space in front. Use 2x or 3x telephoto, if your phone has it, for the columns and carved details.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Rathausplatz (opposite the Burgtheater, across the Ring). The Burgtheater's lower front façade framed by the open town hall square, with the theatre filling the view across the Ringstrasse. From here the lower front of the theatre is framed by the open square, with the building filling the view across the Ringstraße. The theatre is to the north-east of you.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and keep the horizontal lines of the façade level with the grid, so the building does not lean. Put the theatre in the middle third and leave a little foreground of open square. For a different view, try Universitätsring for the full front with a tram passing, or the Volksgarten edge for the theatre framed by trees.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the façade to focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly so the lit front doesn't glare. After dark, use night mode and hold the phone against a railing or your elbows to keep it still.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: After dark, when the illuminated façade is a favourite. Daytime also works well if the square is not crowded.

text.access_note: The outside can be photographed from public streets and squares, but check the official site before you go for visits inside, and note that photography is not allowed during performances.

text.description:
The Volksoper is Vienna's 'people's opera', a theatre that stages opera, operetta, musicals and ballet. It opened in 1898 as a civic theatre for plays, built in only ten months to mark an imperial jubilee. It took its present name and its musical focus in the years after 1903. Today it seats around 1,260 people, and its season runs from September to June.

For photographs, the appeal is a big, solid theatre façade on a city street, so it works well as a straightforward record of your day in Vienna. You can include a bit of street life around it to give a sense of scale. Film fans may like to know that the building appeared in the 1987 James Bond film The Living Daylights, standing in for a conservatory in Bratislava. The interior scenes were filmed elsewhere.

The building is large, so the main challenge is fitting it in. Stepping back to the far side of the street usually helps, and you can use the ultra-wide lens if there is no room to go further. Keep your phone level so the vertical lines of the façade don't lean, and watch for passing traffic and people crossing the frame. Check the official site before you go if you want to see a performance or the inside.
text.geographic_location: The Volksoper stands on Währinger Straße in Vienna, on the north-western side of the city centre. A confectioner's shop called Zum süßen Eck sits directly across the street.
text.directions_text: No Underground or tram stop is listed for this spot, so start from the centre of Vienna and head north-west towards Währinger Straße, by your usual local transport or on foot. Look for 'Volksoper' on your map. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) because the building is large and you will be quite close. Switch to the default lens (1x) once you have stepped back across the street, for a more natural look with less stretching at the edges.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. The building is much wider than that, so for the full façade, walk back across Währinger Straße and turn to face the theatre.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line the base of the façade up with a horizontal line, so the walls stay upright. Leave a little space above the roof and include some street at the bottom to show the scale. For detail shots, use the telephoto lens (2x-5x, depending on your phone) on the entrance and the decoration above it.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the façade to focus, then slide the exposure down a little if the sky is bright, so the walls keep their detail. In the evening, let night mode work and hold the phone steady against a wall or railing.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Daytime gives clear detail on the façade. Early evening, when the building is lit and people are arriving for a performance, is good for atmosphere. Performances are given from September to June.

text.access_note: The outside can be photographed from the street, but entering the theatre needs a performance ticket or a visit arranged with the venue, so check the official site before you go.

text.description:
The MuseumsQuartier, often shortened to MQ, is a large cultural area of about 9 hectares in Vienna's 7th district. It mixes Baroque buildings with modern architecture by Laurids and Manfred Ortner. The old court stables were renovated from April 1998, and the quarter opened in two stages in June and September 2001. Today it holds big names such as the Leopold Museum, MUMOK and the Kunsthalle Wien, plus the Tanzquartier, the Architekturzentrum Wien and a children's museum.

It photographs well because old and new stand side by side. A historic frontage can sit next to a plain modern block in the same picture, which gives a strong sense of the place. The phone icon on the map is about 20 m south-west of the numbered pin. So you are standing among the buildings rather than looking at them from far away. Turn slowly on the spot and you will find several different views.

For a phone, the space is the challenge. Use the ultra-wide lens (0.5x) to fit in the width of a building, and switch to the default lens (1x) or a little zoom for tidier details such as windows, rooflines and signs. Gridlines help keep the vertical edges straight. People will often be in your frame, so wait a moment for a gap, or use them to show how big the place is. Which parts are open and which need a ticket can change.
text.geographic_location: In Vienna's 7th district, right beside the Museumsquartier U-Bahn station on line U2 and close to Volkstheater station.
text.directions_text: Take the U-Bahn to Museumsquartier station on line U2, which is next to the complex. Volkstheater station is the other nearby stop. The main subject point lies about 21 metres to the north-east of it. The phone icon on the map is about 20 m south-west of the numbered pin. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide lens (0.5x) for the wide open space and the broad building fronts. Then switch to the default lens (1x) for a more natural view, and use telephoto (2x or more, depending on your phone) for details on the upper parts of the buildings.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 20 m south-west of the numbered pin, at the phone icon on the map, and face north-east.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Look for a frame that shows both a Baroque building and a modern one, since that contrast is what the place is about. Turn on gridlines and line them up with the vertical edges of the buildings so they do not lean. Keep the horizon level, and leave some space around people rather than cutting them off at the edge.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on a building to set focus, then slide the exposure down a little if the sky is bright, so the walls do not wash out. If a wide shot looks crowded, try a closer one with the default lens (1x) or a little zoom.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early in the day is usually calmer, with fewer people in your frame. Soft daylight suits the buildings better than harsh midday sun.

text.access_note: The MuseumsQuartier is a cultural complex with several museums, so which parts are open to walk through and which need a ticket can vary; check the official site before you go.

name: Wiener Riesenrad

camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Hauptallee' (2 web pages); placed at the stretch of Hauptallee nearest the subject (our map tiles).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/97979331: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Giant Ferris Wheel' (64 m across).
notes: Historic giant Ferris wheel at the Prater.

text.description:
The Wiener Riesenrad is the big white-and-red Ferris wheel at the entrance to the Prater amusement park in Leopoldstadt, Vienna's 2nd district. It went up in 1897 to mark Emperor Franz Josef I's Golden Jubilee, and it stands about 65 metres tall. From 1920 until 1985 it was the tallest Ferris wheel still standing anywhere. After wartime damage it was rebuilt with 15 gondolas rather than the original 30, so the wheel looks lighter and more open than you might expect.

The square at the base is usually busy, so this spot takes a calmer approach. Stand back on the Hauptallee, the long avenue, and let the chestnut trees frame the wheel. Leaves in the foreground add depth and give the picture a sense of place, and the wheel sits neatly in the gap between the trunks. It is a wider and less crowded shot than the usual close-up at the entrance.

Keep the wheel central and leave a little sky above it. Gridlines help keep the avenue straight, so the trees don't lean. Take a few frames, as people and gondolas drift through the scene. If you want a second picture, walk closer afterwards and point up at the iron latticework from Wiener Riesenradplatz, or include the entrance gates as you arrive from Praterstern.
text.geographic_location: In Leopoldstadt, Vienna's 2nd district, at the entrance to the Prater amusement park.
text.directions_text: From the centre of Vienna, head for the Prater in Leopoldstadt and aim for the Riesenrad at the park entrance. Stand there and look north-east to see the wheel framed by the trees. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) so the trees and the wheel both fit. If the wheel looks small, try telephoto (2x or more, depending on your phone) to bring it closer between the trunks. At Wiener Riesenradplatz, switch to ultra-wide (0.5x).
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Hauptallee (shot from the avenue at some distance from the wheel). The wheel framed between the chestnut trees of the long avenue, with foliage in the foreground. The wheel is to the north-east, and you see it framed between the chestnut trees of the long avenue, with foliage in the foreground. Stay on the avenue rather than walking up to the base, as the distance is what gives the framing.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Switch on gridlines and put the wheel in the middle of the gap between the trees, with a little sky above. Keep the phone level so the avenue doesn't tilt. Let a few leaves overhang the top corners. For a different view, go to Wiener Riesenradplatz, tilt the phone upwards with the ultra-wide lens (0.5x) and fill the frame with the iron latticework and sky.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the wheel to focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the sky and any lights don't wash out. At dusk, use night mode and hold the phone steady against a tree or railing. People walking past will blur, so take several shots.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Sunset or dusk, when the light is soft and the wheel lights up. Warm evenings and weekends are busy, so go on a weekday if you can.

text.access_note: The Hauptallee is a public avenue and you can photograph the wheel from outside it for free; riding the wheel is a paid attraction, so check the official site before you go.
